name: Paternalistic Conservatism
summary: Paternalistic conservatism holds that society is an organic, hierarchical whole in which the privileged owe duties of care to those below, from the feudal idea of noblesse oblige. It uses a benevolent state to keep a safety net, regulate industry and win workers' loyalty, in order to prevent class conflict and revolution, while keeping a market economy, property, monarchy and religion. It is pragmatic and gradualist, rejecting both laissez-faire and socialist planning.
scope: Disraeli's Tory paternalism and Victorian factory reform (Oastler, Sadler, Shaftesbury) and Bismarck's state-led social insurance, with later one-nation and Christian-social heirs. Excludes the free-market right and authoritarian cases such as Chiang's regime. Modern social and foreign-policy issues were mostly not addressed and are low-confidence inferences.

keyFigures.name: Benjamin Disraeli
keyFigures.role: Architect of one-nation Toryism, author of Sybil and Conservative prime minister.

keyFigures.name: Otto von Bismarck
keyFigures.role: Chancellor who built Germany's compulsory social insurance partly to undercut socialism.

keyFigures.name: Anthony Ashley-Cooper, 7th Earl of Shaftesbury
keyFigures.role: Early Tory advocate of Factory Acts and humane treatment of workers.

universal-healthcare.rationale: Bismarck's compulsory sickness insurance and the safety-net role the tradition gives the state point to state-guaranteed care, though the model is insurance-based rather than tax-funded.

markets-allocate-better.rationale: The tradition keeps a market economy but wants regulation and a safety net, rejecting laissez-faire as the free-market right's critics note; it does not say markets always beat government.

tax-the-wealthy.rationale: It supports some redistribution but also defends hierarchy and property, and gives no figure; the elite's duty is framed as care rather than heavy taxation.

unions-good.rationale: Disraeli's government passed trade union laws and the tradition wants workers' loyalty to society, so unions are welcomed as legitimate when they cooperate rather than fight classes.

property-fundamental.rationale: Conservatives defend property as a bulwark of order and the paternalist duty of owners presupposes ownership, though property is conditional on its obligations.

regulate-corporations.rationale: The tradition favours regulation that serves consumers and producers and protects workers, as in the Factory Acts championed by Shaftesbury and Oastler.

cut-welfare.rationale: A social safety net against poverty is the heart of the ideology; Bismarck built social insurance precisely to give workers a stake in the order.

worker-ownership.rationale: It rejects socialist ownership schemes and accepts hierarchy between owners and workers, wanting duty rather than workers' control.

strong-leader.rationale: It favours established institutions and gradual change over a leader bypassing them, though authority is valued; Bismarck's strong-minister model is an exception.

state-harmful.rationale: The state is cast as a benevolent paternal figure that sets goals and maintains a safety net, and Bismarck used it for insurance, so calling it unnecessary or harmful is the opposite stance.

limit-guns.rationale: Never addressed; paternal order favours restriction while rural conservatives resist, so adherents split.

empower-police-military.rationale: Order and strong institutions are central to the Tory case, and Disraeli prized the army and empire; support is moderate not extreme.

traditional-family.rationale: Conservatives place faith in family, property and religion as the base of organic society.

more-religion-public.rationale: Religion is treated as a binding force in the tradition, from Stoecker's Protestant workers' party to Coleridge's national church, so a larger public role is welcomed.

correct-racial-injustice.rationale: Paternal duty to the disadvantaged could support redress, but the strand is class-based and never addressed this; adherents split.

preserve-national-culture.rationale: Disraeli named maintaining the country's institutions as the Tory party's first object, in the Crystal Palace speech.

gradual-change.rationale: Burke's view that a state without means of change lacks means of conservation, and organic development, are core to conservatism and to paternalist reform from above.

reduce-immigration.rationale: Never a defining question for the strand; one-nation unity is inclusive of those inside the nation but adherents divide on numbers.

free-trade.rationale: Disraeli favoured an imperial tariff, while later paternalists accepted free trade; the strand is divided and pragmatic.

nation-first.rationale: The speech frames the choice as an imperial England against continental cosmopolitan principles, and the national community is the object of paternal duty.

drastic-climate-action.rationale: Never addressed; state paternalism favours action but conservative caution and cost concerns divide adherents.

tech-solves-problems.rationale: Conservatives put prudence and inherited institutions ahead of faith in progress, yet the tradition is not hostile to technology; no stated view.

revolution-justified.rationale: Nulled (statement review, 2026-11-12): the old wording asked whether revolution is sometimes justified, and this disagreement rested on a preference for reform or lawful means, which doesn't say revolution is never justified.

reviewHistory.rationale: The pragmatic argument is that elite duty prevents revolution; the whole strand aims to forestall it.

central-planning.rationale: The article states it rejects command or planned economies and public control of means of production.

basic-income.rationale: Paternalist welfare is conditional and structured, as in Bismarck's contribution-based insurance, rather than unconditional cash.

tariffs-protect-industry.rationale: Disraeli backed imperial tariffs while the strand later embraced free trade; adherents split by period.

state-directs-investment.rationale: Japanese LDP paternalism was interventionist but British paternalists were not; split by country.

widespread-small-property.rationale: Property is valued, but the strand does not target concentration versus dispersal.

abolish-money-wages.rationale: The tradition keeps a market-based mixed economy and rejects public control of the means of production.

abolish-central-banks.rationale: A regulated market economy with a state role is assumed; free-market monetary radicalism is the opposite pole.

corporatist-bargaining.rationale: Nulled (statement review, 2026-11-11): its rationale is about price setting, and the statement now asks only about setting wages.

reviewHistory.rationale: Bismarck's occupational employer organizations that administered accident insurance resemble corporatism, but no general demand for price-setting bodies exists.
reviewHistory.author: claude-sonnet-5-5

reviewHistory.rationale: Nulled (statement review, 2026-11-11): its rationale is about price setting, and the statement now asks only about setting wages.

one-party-rule.rationale: The strand grows from parliamentary Toryism; only some authoritarian cases such as Chiang's regime blur this, so it is not central.

monarchy-legitimate.rationale: Disraeli's Tory aim of maintaining the country's institutions includes the Crown, and Bismarck served the Kaiser.

democracy-best.rationale: Tory democracy accepted the vote but the tradition accepts hierarchy and benevolent authority; adherents hold varied views.

direct-votes.rationale: Burke-style conservatism limits participation to the qualified and prefers representative government to plebiscites.

workers-councils.rationale: Political power grounded in workers' own councils overturns the hierarchy in which elites carry duties to those below, so it is rejected.

right-to-secede.rationale: Disraeli feared breakup of the empire and the organic nation is treated as an inseparable whole.

natural-rulers.rationale: Social hierarchy is accepted as natural, with elites carrying duties to those below.

separate-church-state.rationale: Coleridge's national church and religion as a pillar of order oppose strict separation.

laws-from-scripture.rationale: Religion is valued as a moral base but legal codes are inherited custom rather than scriptural rule.

private-courts-defense.rationale: The state has a positive duty to maintain order and promote welfare; privatising its core functions contradicts it.

ethnic-nation.rationale: One-nation framing unites classes within existing national institutions rather than defining nation by ethnicity.

equal-outcomes.rationale: Hierarchy is accepted as natural; paternalism offers a floor not equality.

civilizational-union.rationale: Nation-centred outlook; Disraeli opposed dissolution of imperial unity into other blocs.

self-interest-moral.rationale: Noblesse oblige holds that privilege brings duties to others, so pursuit of self-interest is not praised as a virtue.

duties-before-rights.rationale: Scruton-style conservatism says individual liberty is not absolute, and noblesse oblige centres on duty.

nature-intrinsic-value.rationale: The conservatism covered in the SEP stresses family, property and religion rather than nature's own worth; adherents are split and the topic is rarely addressed.

industrial-civilization-disaster.rationale: Coleridge criticised unchecked industrialisation, but the tradition reforms industrial society rather than rejecting it.

accelerate-technology.rationale: Oakeshott prefers stability to improvement and conservatives distrust disruption of institutions.

unbreakable-encryption.rationale: A modern issue where paternal security concerns pull one way and conservative respect for private life the other, so adherents split.

restore-past-order.rationale: Conservatism values continuity but paternalists reform to adapt; no desire to restore a lost order.

results-over-ideology.rationale: The article notes its pragmatism and critics call it non-ideological, though adherents hold paternal principles.

direct-action.rationale: Order and reform from above, not pressure from the street, are the method.

return-to-foraging.rationale: Organic civilisation and its institutions are what is to be preserved.

abolish-division-of-labor.rationale: The tradition accepts an industrial market economy and natural social hierarchy, so ending the division of labour is far outside it.

distribute-by-need.rationale: Care for the poor is a floor but distribution mainly by station and market.

production-for-use.rationale: It keeps a market-based mixed economy rather than replacing profit-led production with planned production for need.

profit-exploitation.rationale: The strand rejects socialist analysis; profit is legitimate if owners meet duties.

dictatorship-of-proletariat.rationale: Working-class rule over former elites reverses the paternal order where a governing class cares for those beneath it.

collective-farming.rationale: Rejection of public control of the means of production and defence of property rules out compulsory collectivised agriculture.

taxation-theft.rationale: A paternal state funds a social safety net through public revenue, so taxation is legitimate rather than robbery.

harm-principle.rationale: The paternal state promotes the morality and welfare of subjects, not only prevention of harm.

individual-rights-only.rationale: Organic society puts the community and mutual obligations before individualist rights.

exit-over-voice.rationale: Obligations bind members of an organic society; exit is not the check.

state-as-business.rationale: The state is a paternal figure with duties, not a firm with customers.

positive-liberty.rationale: Freedom is tied to authority and welfare in this tradition rather than mere non-interference.

total-state.rationale: It accepts a benevolent state but also faith in family, property and religion, not state direction of all life.

national-rebirth.rationale: Paternalists want to reform an existing order gradually and avert unrest, not rebuild the nation through radical rebirth.

territorial-expansion.rationale: Disraeli prized maintaining the empire rather than conquering more, and the tradition is not defined by expansion, so adherents split.

personal-loyalty-rule.rationale: Noblesse oblige echoes feudal ideas but modern paternalism works via state institutions.

bound-labor.rationale: Elites owe care, but modern paternalists do not support legal bondage.

universal-morality.rationale: Burke's inherited wisdom is customary, but religious paternalists hold moral truths; split.

revive-national-language.rationale: The tradition values national institutions and culture but takes no documented stand on reviving a lapsed language.

workplace-democracy.rationale: Hierarchy in the workplace is accepted, with duties rather than votes.

economic-freedom.rationale: Disputes the claim that economic liberty alone sustains freedom; state regulation is accepted.

rule-by-example.rationale: Noblesse oblige holds that the privileged lead by responsible example, alongside law.

national-self-determination.rationale: Imperial Toryism valued the empire's unity yet nations' institutions; no clear stand and adherents split.

reason-over-faith.rationale: Burke defended prejudice and custom as latent wisdom and religion as social foundation, against reason as sole guide.

work-for-welfare.rationale: Bismarck's insurance was contribution-based, but modern adherents divide on conditionality.

class-collaboration.rationale: Obligations across classes to avert conflict are explicit in Disraeli's two nations concern.

sacrifice-heritage.rationale: Disraeli named maintaining the institutions of the country as the Tory party's first object, so sacrificing inherited institutions is rejected.

workers-nation.rationale: Stoecker and Bismarck sought workers' attachment to nation and monarchy.

distinct-gender-roles.rationale: Traditionalist roots favour inherited roles, but modern paternalists accept equality in public life, so adherents split.

state-class-instrument.rationale: It treats the state as a benevolent father to all classes, not an instrument of class domination, which is a Marxist claim.

assimilate-immigrants.rationale: Organic nation favours shared culture but strand is silent; adherents split.

national-mission.rationale: Disraeli's imperial vision was of maintaining empire, not of exporting a political system; adherents split.

political-elite-corrupt.rationale: The ideology depends on a governing class that is competent and dutiful, so it rejects the picture of corrupt, out-of-touch elites.

security-forces-accountable.rationale: Never addressed; deference to authority and respect for rule of law pull in different directions.

night-watchman-state.rationale: The paternal state sets goals, ensures fair play and keeps a safety net, going well beyond a minimal state.

consent-of-governed.rationale: Authority legitimate when paternal; Burke ties it to tradition; split.

trade-surplus.rationale: Disraeli favoured imperial tariffs yet the strand has no doctrine on trade balances; adherents split.

population-transfer.rationale: Forced removal of minorities is at odds with the aim of binding all classes into one nation.

initiating-force-wrong.rationale: Conservatives accept state force for order and authority; the absolute prohibition is a libertarian principle.

competition-drives-progress.rationale: The strand stresses cooperation among classes and reciprocal duty over struggle between individuals or peoples.

separated-powers.rationale: Burke-style conservatism values balanced institutions and checks over unconstrained power.

vanguard-party.rationale: A revolutionary party leading the working class is opposite to the paternal approach that prevents revolution through elite reform.

priority-to-poor.rationale: Disraeli warned that the ruling class must respond to hardship, and the tradition stresses duty to those below.

right-to-buy-council-homes.rationale: Wider ownership appeals to Tories but paternal care for tenants pulls the other way; nothing states a position.

restrict-strikes-picketing.rationale: The tradition has both backed union legalisation (Disraeli) and order, so adherents split on limits.

diversity-weakens-cohesion.rationale: The one-nation concern is class cohesion, and sources give no view on ethnic diversity; adherents split.

offices-by-lottery.rationale: Rule by lot ignores qualification and station, which Burke-style conservatism requires of those who govern.

price-controls-essentials.rationale: A regulated mixed economy permits market intervention, but nothing states support for fixed maximum prices; adherents divide on it.

party-controls-media.rationale: Party control of information belongs to single-party regimes, which the tradition does not endorse.

party-commands-army.rationale: The tradition has the army under the Crown or state, not a ruling party.

party-discipline-binding.rationale: Not a documented principle for this tradition, whose pragmatism runs toward flexibility.

pool-sovereignty.rationale: Disraeli preferred maintained national and imperial institutions to merging into continental arrangements.

head-commands-forces.rationale: Bismarck's Kaiser commanded the forces while British paternalists accept parliamentary government; split by country.

church-by-bishops.rationale: Coleridge's national church and the hierarchical, organic conception of society favour episcopal order.

clerical-rule.rationale: Religion supports political order in this tradition but statesmen like Disraeli and Bismarck ruled, not clergy.

defeat-own-government-war.rationale: The nation-first, imperial outlook treats loyalty in war as a duty, never as working for defeat.

censor-art-for-virtue.rationale: The paternal state promotes subjects' morality, yet traditions of free expression divide adherents.

recall-officials.rationale: Recall is a plebiscitary check on representatives, which Burke-style conservatism rejects.

end-foreign-alliances.rationale: Disraeli's vision of an engaged imperial Britain is opposed to withdrawal.

rural-life-healthier.rationale: Organic traditionalism sometimes praises country life, but the tradition is fundamentally about managing industrial towns.

reunify-divided-nation.rationale: Bismarck unified Germany, but the strand has no general doctrine on reunification; adherents split.

cultures-equal-different.rationale: Disraeli's imperial outlook assumed hierarchy among civilizations.

encourage-eccentricity.rationale: Conservatives treat custom as latent wisdom, against Mill's view that conformity harms development.

constituent-assembly.rationale: Burke-style conservatism opposes rewriting constitutions afresh instead of letting them develop organically.

restrict-freedoms-for-growth.rationale: Chiang's regime is cited as paternal authoritarian, but mainstream adherents do not make this central.

rich-countries-aid-poor.rationale: Elite duty is framed within the nation, so no stated view on global aid; adherents split.

direct-election-head-of-state.rationale: Disraeli and Bismarck served hereditary monarchs and the tradition favours inherited heads of state.

central-bank-independence.rationale: Never addressed; adherents split between state oversight and monetary stability.

property-serves-common-good.rationale: The paternal tradition holds that the privileged owe duties to those below, making property a trust rather than an absolute right.

nonpartisan-head-of-state.rationale: Institutions of the country, including the Crown, are meant to stand for national unity above class and faction.

force-to-prevent-secession.rationale: Disraeli feared imperial dissolution, but the strand has no stated doctrine; split.

character-from-environment.rationale: Elite duty to relieve hardship presumes circumstances shape people, though traditionalist views stress inherited nature.

sovereign-above-law.rationale: Burke-style constitutionalism opposes a ruler unbound by law.

mixed-constitution.rationale: Burke-influenced conservatism favours balance of orders and institutions of both elite and popular kinds.

leader-cult.rationale: Cult of the leader as embodiment of the nation is alien to institution-based conservatism.

land-redistribution.rationale: Landed property and its duties are defended, so confiscation for redistribution is rejected.

refugee-return.rationale: Never addressed in sources; adherents split.

women-must-cover.rationale: Not part of the documented tradition and at odds with its Western institutional setting.

common-currency.rationale: Never addressed; adherents split between pooling and national monetary control.

kin-peoples-union.rationale: The tradition centres on the existing nation and empire, not cross-border unions of kin peoples.

national-cultural-autonomy.rationale: One-nation framing wants a single national community, not separate self-governing minorities.

material-conditions-drive-history.rationale: Burke and Disraeli stress institutions, moral duty and tradition, against economic determinism.

no-bailouts.rationale: Never addressed; paternal state protectiveness conflicts with market discipline, so adherents split.

economic-self-sufficiency.rationale: Disraeli favoured an imperial tariff, but a closed bloc shut off from outside trade goes beyond the tradition.

moral-incentives.rationale: Duty is emphasised but wages and material incentives remain in the market economy; adherents split.

history-own-civilization.rationale: Preserving national institutions and traditions favours teaching history centred on the nation.

capitalism-adapts.rationale: Disraeli's pragmatic argument is that reform answers hardship and preserves the order against revolutionary collapse.

freedom-to-discriminate.rationale: Regulation serving consumers and producers and a paternal view of fair play oppose unrestricted refusal of service.

noblesse-oblige.rationale: Wikipedia's definition (s1) puts particular emphasis on the paternalistic obligation, after the feudal noblesse oblige, of the privileged and wealthy toward the poorer parts of society; Disraeli warned that a ruling class that ignores hardship invites revolution.

animal-suffering-matters.rationale: Victorian reformers such as Shaftesbury supported animal protection; not a core paternalist theme.

institutions-fit-civilization.rationale: Burkean conservatism, which this strand draws on, holds that institutions grow from a people's history and cannot simply be transplanted.

office-by-exam.rationale: Adherents split between the traditional view that office suits the gentry and the Victorian reform of merit-based civil service; the doctrine does not settle it.

recallable-delegates.rationale: Nulled (statement review, 2026-11-11): its value turns on whether representatives must follow binding instructions, and the statement now asks only whether voters can recall them at any time.

reviewHistory.rationale: Burkean tradition holds that representatives exercise independent judgment rather than act as instructed delegates, and it favours hierarchy and gradual change.
reviewHistory.author: claude-sonnet-5-5

reviewHistory.rationale: Nulled (statement review, 2026-11-11): its value turns on whether representatives must follow binding instructions, and the statement now asks only whether voters can recall them at any time.

individual-pension-accounts.rationale: Bismarck's pay-as-you-go-style state social insurance and the tradition's rejection of laissez-faire favour collective state provision over private individual accounts.

land-use-tenure.rationale: The tradition keeps private property and inherited landed hierarchy while rejecting socialist planning, so it opposes use-based communal tenure.

foreign-land-ownership.rationale: The doctrine does not address the issue and adherents are split between national-property instincts and respect for property rights.

job-guarantee.rationale: It built a safety net and factory regulation but kept the market economy, and never promised work to all.

no-duty-to-obey.rationale: It treats society as an organic hierarchy that wins loyalty through duties of care, so obedience to the established order is expected.

abolish-legal-marriage.rationale: It keeps the church, monarchy and family as institutions of the organic society.

religious-nation.rationale: Disraeli backed the established church yet accepted Jews and others in the nation; adherents split.

women-equality-needs-economic-change.rationale: The tradition defends the family and keeps the existing order; it seeks reform of conditions through paternal duty, not transformation of the economic system.

cooperative-communities.rationale: The tradition is hierarchical and monarchist and keeps property and the state, so communities holding property in common contradict it.

majority-settlement.rationale: Disraeli's one-nation idea stresses unity but there is no doctrine on steering settlement into minority regions; adherents split.

historical-land-claim.rationale: The tradition's concern is class duty, not land claims; adherents are split and the sources are silent.

criminalize-homosexuality.rationale: Victorian adherents accepted such laws, while modern one-nation heirs mostly do not; the doctrine is silent so it is a split.

alienated-labor.rationale: Factory reformers such as Oastler and Shaftesbury attacked harsh conditions, but they did not use the Marxist concept; split.

islam-incompatible.rationale: The tradition did not address it and modern heirs are split.

social-market-economy.rationale: It keeps a market economy with a safety net and industrial regulation, rejecting both laissez-faire and state planning, which is this statement.

stay-neutral-between-blocs.rationale: The tradition did not address it and heirs are split between alliances and independence.

state-promotes-atheism.rationale: It treats the established church and religion as supports of the organic society, so promoting atheism is opposed.

abolish-police-prisons.rationale: It stands for order and the maintenance of national institutions, so abolishing police and prisons is rejected.

charity-over-state-aid.rationale: It holds that the state and the upper classes have a duty to provide a safety net, as Disraeli's reforms and Bismarck's social insurance show, rather than leaving the poor to charity alone.

income-for-work-not-ownership.rationale: It defends property and a market economy while asking the privileged to care for others, so it rejects the claim that returns on ownership are unearned.

never-kill-self-defence.rationale: It is an order-defending tradition with no pacifist strand, and the state's use of force and self-defence are accepted.

unbroken-national-continuity.rationale: Its organic view of society rests on inherited institutions and a historic national community, as in Disraeli's appeal to national history and institutions.

politics-spiritual-struggle.rationale: It is pragmatic and gradualist, aiming to avoid class conflict through reform rather than frame politics as cosmic struggle.

socialism-needs-workers-power.rationale: The ideology preserves hierarchy and property to prevent class conflict and rejects socialist planning.

local-essentials-public.rationale: A benevolent state that regulates industry and provides services is core; public health and sanitation reform were Disraelian measures.

municipal-property.rationale: It keeps a market economy and property while rejecting socialist planning, so community ownership of production is rejected.

person-over-state.rationale: It speaks of duties within an organic whole, so it denies pure individualism but also holds the state should care for each person; split.

spiritual-nature.rationale: Religion and an organic moral order are part of the tradition, and Disraeli tied Toryism to church and national institutions.

racial-pride.rationale: Disraeli stressed national pride, but pride specifically in race is not a position the sources record.

defensive-wars-only.rationale: Disraeli's Crystal Palace speech defends maintaining empire, so strictly defensive use of arms is rejected.

foreign-partition-plot.rationale: The tradition did not address plots against the nation, and adherents' views vary with the period; no inference stronger than neutral.

soldiers-refuse-war.rationale: The tradition defends hierarchy, duty and empire (Disraeli's Crystal Palace speech), so refusing orders in inter-state wars goes against it.

collective-bargaining.rationale: Disraeli's reforms legalised peaceful picketing and Victorian factory reform protected workers, and paternalists sought workers' loyalty, but they preferred a harmony of classes to union power.

smash-state-machine.rationale: The tradition is gradualist and uses the existing state, as in Bismarck's and Disraeli's reforms, precisely to prevent revolution.

free-economic-experiment.rationale: It prefers a managed, organic social order with state regulation and a safety net, not an open field of economic systems with no blueprint.

sacred-nation.rationale: It sees society as an organic whole bound across generations, and Disraeli stressed the nation and empire, but the focus is on class duties more than on the nation as sacred.

workers-own-party.rationale: Bismarck's social insurance was designed to wean workers from the socialist party, and one-nation Toryism seeks to win workers within the existing order.

women-property-inheritance.rationale: Victorian paternalists defended a hierarchical family order; modern heirs accept equality, so adherents are split.

democracy-is-procedure.rationale: Disraeli extended the vote pragmatically but the tradition prizes duty and organic order over procedure; adherents split.

negative-income-tax.rationale: The tradition wants a paternal safety net with duties and in-kind services, not a market-style cash substitute; Bismarck used insurance schemes.

defend-planned-state.rationale: The tradition rejects socialist planning while keeping a market economy and property.

national-church-status.rationale: Disraeli defended national institutions including the established Church.

self-ownership.rationale: Paternalist conservatism holds that society is an organic hierarchical whole with duties owed, not a collection of self-owning individuals.

targeted-social-spending.rationale: Bismarck's insurance was tied to workers and employers rather than means-tested, while safety nets for the poor were also backed; adherents are split.

financial-transactions-tax.rationale: The tradition predates such taxes and accepts state regulation of industry while keeping markets, so no commitment can be drawn from the sources.

labour-theory-of-value.rationale: The tradition rejects socialist planning and class conflict, and keeps a market economy and property; it treats labour as owed fair treatment rather than as the sole source of value.

market-under-party-rule.rationale: Bismarck's welfare measures were framed as a defence against socialism, and the tradition rejects socialist planning, so it denies that a communist party could build socialism through markets.

decent-living-guarantee.rationale: A social safety net against poverty is the heart of the ideology; Bismarck built social insurance precisely to give workers a stake in the order. (Carried over from cut-welfare, "Welfare programs create dependency and should be cut.", with the value reversed, 2026-11-11.)

missingStatements.text: The wealthy and privileged have a duty to look after those less fortunate than themselves.
missingStatements.rationale: Noblesse oblige is the defining principle of the tradition, and Disraeli warned that a ruling class that ignores hardship invites revolution.

notes: Strongly contested between Tory and German strands and with free-market critics who call it right-wing socialism. Sources s3 and s4 were read in part only. Disraeli favoured imperial tariffs while later paternalists accepted free trade.
